section.title: Chapter review and discovery problems
section.p: The chapter began with a familiar quotient:
That quotient measured average change. By shrinking the interval, we found a new number:
The same number appeared in several forms. It was an instantaneous rate, a tangent slope, the coefficient in the best linear approximation, and velocity when the function was position.

figure.caption: The derivative is one idea with several connected meanings.

section.p: The problems below are meant to make those meanings fluent. Some ask for calculations. Some ask for explanations. Some ask for judgment. Calculus needs all three.

exercise.title: Why is the derivative one idea with several meanings?

statement.p: The same number f'(a) is an instantaneous rate, a tangent slope, a linearization coefficient, and a velocity when the function is position. In your own words, why are those not four different inventions, and what shared limiting process ties them together?

hint.p: Each meaning starts from an average comparison and shrinks the interval. The limit of those averages is the derivative.

exercise.title: Why is the derivative both local and stronger than continuity?

statement.p: Differentiability at a is about nearby slopes, and it forces continuity at a. In your own words, why is the derivative a local idea, and why can a continuous graph still fail to have a tangent slope?

hint.p: The difference quotient only looks near one input. Nearby heights can agree while nearby slopes do not.

subsection.title: Hook: why the definition is not enough
subsection.p: The derivative definition is the source of everything in this chapter:
It tells us what the derivative means. It proves the first formulas. It catches corners, cusps, and jumps. It explains velocity, tangent slope, and local linear approximation.
But it is too slow to use from scratch every time.
With the tools of this chapter, we could expand first:
Then we can differentiate term by term:
That works here because the product is a polynomial. But expansion is not always possible or pleasant. What about
These functions are built from simpler pieces by multiplying, dividing, and composing. Their derivatives should be built from the derivatives of those pieces.
The next chapter turns the definition into a working language. The goal is not to replace meaning with rules. The goal is to make the meaning fast enough to use.

exercise.title: Why is the definition the source, but not enough by itself?

statement.p: The limit definition tells what the derivative means and catches corners, yet it is too slow for everyday products, quotients, and compositions. In your own words, why must the next chapter keep the meaning while building a faster language?

hint.p: Expanding a product into a polynomial is not always possible. The derivative of a built function should be built from the derivatives of the pieces.
